articleTitle: Design essentials to achieve a specific SIL
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: This paper provides a PowerPoint presentation providing an overview of the concept of a safety integrity level (SIL) and its importance in the structure and compliance requirements within IEC 61508 and associated standards. In particular, the presentation outlines the following: the failure categories within IEC 61508 (systematic failures and random hardware failures) and of their relationship to the concept of SIL; the reason why we need the concept of SIL; the relationship of SIL to achievement of the tolerable risk frequency; the concept of modes of operation and how this impacts on SIL determination. The presentation provides an understanding of the key concepts sufficient to support other presentations being given.

articleTitle: SIL Determination and the application of LOPA
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: For a number of years, industry has been trying to apply the principles outlined in IEC 61508. In the process industry, this has resulted in a focus on the requirements of IEC 61511. In the field of SIL determination, IEC 61511 provides suggestions of a number of different techniques - these are shown in IEC 61511-3. These include event trees, risk graphs, safety matrices, fault trees and layer of protection analysis (LOPA). In the first few years, industry embraced the use of risk graphs as the method of choice. Over time, many companies have used this method and found that it was (a) giving higher safety integrity level targets than really needed and (b) was less flexible than other methods and so more difficult to use in many cases. This has resulted in a general move to other methods and in particular to the use of LOPA. However, there are a number of pitfalls in the use of the LOPA method that have become evident through its use. This presentation will review the application of LOPA and highlight a number of the pitfalls and misuse of LOPA that we have found to be in current practice.

articleTitle: SIL determination: Pitfalls found in LOPA studies
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: This paper introduced the study of protection analysis layer that is used to provide a more consistent approach to safety integrity level (SIL) assessment suggested by the Buncefield Standards Task Group (BSTG). The LOPA method has been adopted by industry, which has submitted LOPA studies for its fuel storage overfill prevention systems to the health and safety executive (HSE) for . This talk presents and discusses a number of example issues identified in the LOPA studies looked at by HSL.

articleTitle: SIL aspects in relationship to Fire and Gas systems
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: The paper will look at a number of aspects in determining the safety requirements for Fire & Gas system associated with a Oil & Gas production or petrochemical plant. Two approaches will be considered. One approach will be by considering the number of general cases and determining a general SIL target for Fire & Gas safety loops, the other approach will be to undertake a SIL targeting exercise for each of the plant location and determine the requirements using LOPA. Clearly for the safety loops to be effective, not only will they have to met the require reliability but the detectors have correctly located and the paper will also include examples of dispersion modelling to assist in the location of gas detectors.

publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: The IEC 61508 and IEC 61511 requires common cause to be considered during safety system design. Common cause between redundant elements within the safety system can be the most significant factor when calculating the probability of failure on demand. The standards provide guidance on how common cause should be taken into account during system design and there is good recognition among those applying the standard that common cause should be taken into account. The standard also requires safety systems to be independent of other safety measures and independent from causes of demand unless the lack of independence is taken into account. There is however very little advice within the standards on how to take into account dependency issues between the safety systems and causes of demand or between safety systems and other risk reduction measures. This can be a dominant issue when determining SIL particularly in cases where SIL requirements are high or when demand rates are low. This is not well recognised by those who are applying the standard. Examples of where dependency may be significant during SIL determination will be considered together with ways to evaluate the effects.

articleTitle: Reducing risks ALARP and the implications for SIL determination
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: The opening presentation will introduce risk concepts and terminology, and how they are reflected in the UK regulatory system for occupational safety generally. The UK approach to risk management will be outlined and compared with the legal requirement for 'the provision and maintenance of plant and systems of work that are, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe and without risks to health', including risk criteria and how to evaluate any possible risk reduction including gross disproportion. The role of safety instrumented systems in risk reduction, both frequency and consequence, will be outlined as an introduction to the following sessions.

articleTitle: The approach to legacy systems within the non-nuclear power station sector
publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: During 2007 the management of legacy protection systems (ie those developed and implemented prior to the IEC 61508 standard) came to the fore. As almost every UK power station pre-dates the IEC 61508 standard they have a large number of such legacy protection systems to manage - hence the industry sector has a strong interest in this topic. All 9 UK generators have come together to form a technical working group to develop an approach and guidelines for the management of these systems on non- nuclear power stations. One of the principle issues addressed has been whether there is a need to retrospectively apply the whole safety life cycle of IEC 61508 to all of the legacy protection systems within the power stations - the conclusion has been no, only to a representative sample. The presentation will describe the consideration leading to this conclusion and then go through the requirements of the approach and guidelines developed for the non-nuclear power station sector.

publicationTitle: 2008 4th IET Seminar on SIL Determination - Minimising the Risk of Your Systems
abstract: The safety function is a cornerstone of functional safety ... get it wrong and you may have no protection . The SIL of a safety function is a cornerstone of functional safety ... if it is too low you increase the risk . The SIL concept was developed as a parameter to determine the rigour of the measures to be applied to combat systematic failure causes . The SIL is the key parameter for the Architectural Constraints (HFT) and the Systematic Safety Integrity measures (H/W & S/W) . The mode of operation a key aspect of SIL determination
